world_behind.title: The commentary's last chapter
world_behind.text: Nephi's exposition began at chapter 25 by explaining why Isaiah was hard; it ends here. What follows in chapter 31 is a different kind of writing altogether, the doctrine of Christ set out as a procedure. This chapter is the last of the prophetic material and reads like a summation.

world_behind.title: Covenant redefined
world_behind.text: Verse 2 states the rule the rest of the chapter runs on: Gentiles who repent are covenant people, Jews who will not repent are cast off. Lineage sets no floor and no ceiling. After chapters of seed, branches, and remnants, this is the sentence that says what those categories are for.

world_behind.title: Isaiah, quoted from memory of his own copy
world_behind.text: Verses 9 and 11 through 15 repeat Isaiah 11 almost word for word, nine chapters after Nephi copied it out in full. He does not announce the quotation. His readers have the text a few pages back, and the repetition is how he applies it.

world_behind.title: Scales
world_behind.text: The image in verse 6 is of something crusted over the eye flaking away. Paul's sight returns the same way in Acts, with scales falling. It is a physical picture of recognition: nothing is added, something is removed.

world_behind.title: A clock set in generations
world_behind.text: Verse 6 says many generations shall not pass away before the remnant becomes pure, a slow clock by any measure. The chapter's other time markers are equally loose: speedily in verse 10, a long time in verse 18. Nephi is specific about sequence and deliberately vague about dates.

world_behind.title: Two audiences in one chapter
world_behind.text: Verse 1 addresses his beloved brethren; verses 2 through 8 are about Gentiles and Jews in the third person; verse 18 returns to his brethren. The chapter moves between the people in front of him and the peoples he has been shown without marking the transitions. The whole commentary has worked this way.

words.text: Here the verb means allow. Nephi names a conclusion, that his own people are more righteous than the Gentiles, and refuses to let it stand before he says anything else in the chapter. Elsewhere the record uses the same word in its familiar modern sense, of pain borne ("he suffereth the pains of all men", 2 Ne. 9:21).

Delightsome means pleasing, and the chapter says it twice. The remnant become "a pure and a delightsome people" (v. 6) once the record has reached them, and the scattered Jews "become a delightsome people" (v. 7) once they believe in Christ. Both times the word arrives after a change of belief rather than after a fact of descent. Its one use in the Bible attaches the word to a land (Mal. 3:12).

cites.quote: a pure and a delightsome people

spans.text: a pure and a delightsome people

words.text: A belt, and the verse gives two of them: righteousness for the loins and faithfulness for the reins. Nephi is re-quoting Isaiah, and the image dresses the promised ruler in what he is. A girdle is also what a working man tightened before exertion, so the figure is practical before it is ornamental.

A fatling is a young animal being fattened for slaughter. Treated at 2 Nephi 21:6. Its name comes from what will be done to it. The wolf, the leopard, and the lion are named as hunters, the lamb and the kid as what they hunt, and set among them is an animal people were raising for a table. The record counts fatlings elsewhere among a people's property, taxed by King Noah alongside the gold and the grain (Mosiah 11:3). The verse ends the violence between the animals and says nothing about the use the fatling was being kept for.

The verse names two ages: the sucking child, still nursing, and the weaned child, just past it. Weaning was a marked point in a childhood, and in Genesis it is the occasion of a feast (Gen. 21:8). Isaiah sets both ages beside a snake, one playing at the hole and one with a hand on the den, which stretches the promise across the whole span when a child cannot be left alone.

Untied, released. The verb belongs to the sealed book of chapter 27, where a document is closed with a seal that must be broken. Applied to everything sealed upon the earth, it turns a promise about one record into a promise about all withheld knowledge.

phrases.text: Nephi's own people are the ones warned, and the temptation named is comparison. The chapter that follows dismantles the comparison entirely by making repentance the only criterion. Placing the warning first means no reader can take verses 2 through 8 as a promise about their own side.

phrases.term: As many of the Gentiles as will repent
phrases.text: The chapter's governing sentence, and it cuts both ways in the same breath: unrepentant Jews are cast off. Nephi has spent this book on covenant lines, and here he says the Lord "covenanteth with none save it be with them that repent" (v. 2). Descent gets a people to the door; nothing more.

cites.quote: covenanteth with none save it be with them that repent

spans.text: covenanteth with none save it be with them that repent

phrases.term: Their scales of darkness shall begin to fall
phrases.text: Scales are flakes or crusts, the sort that form over a wound or an eye, and here they are called darkness. Recovery of sight is described as removal rather than addition. Saul's blindness ends the same way, when "there fell from his eyes as it had been scales" (Acts 9:18). The verse then attaches a long timescale, many generations, which keeps the image from promising a sudden event.

phrases.term: Commence his work among all nations
phrases.text: To commence is to begin, and the verb does chronological work in a chapter full of future tenses. The restoration is described as a beginning, and its scope is stated in the widest terms the record uses: all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people. Everything the chapter says afterward about peace and knowledge is the consequence of something that starts here.

phrases.term: With righteousness shall the Lord God judge the poor
phrases.text: Nephi reaches back nine chapters and re-quotes his own copy of Isaiah 11 without announcing it. The Isaiah chapter gave a ruler judging with equity for the meek (Isa. 11:4); the same words here are attached to the restoration he has been describing. He applies the prophecy; he does not stop to explain it.

phrases.term: A great division among the people
phrases.text: A division is a separation, and in this verse an enforced one: the wicked destroyed, the righteous spared. It is the chapter's hardest verse, and it is placed deliberately between restoration and peace. Nephi does not present the division as regrettable or as a last resort; he presents it as the mechanism. The peaceable kingdom of the following verses is on the far side of a sorting, not instead of one.

phrases.term: Nothing which is secret save it shall be revealed
phrases.text: Three clauses saying the same thing about secrets, works of darkness, and sealed things. The Lord promises the same in the gospels, that "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed" (Luke 12:2). Read against chapter 27's sealed portion, this verse is the record's own promise that its withheld part is temporary.

phrases.term: Satan shall have power... no more
phrases.text: The chapter's last promise, and it carries a qualifier that is easy to skip: for a long time. Nephi does not say forever. He ends a chapter about restoration with a peace that is real, complete in its own terms, and explicitly bounded.

verses.label: v. 3–6
verses.title: The record predicts its own transmission, step by step
verses.text: The sequence is given as a chain with each link stated: "after the book of which I have spoken shall come forth, and be written unto the Gentiles, and sealed up again unto the Lord," then it goes to the remnant, then "shall the remnant of our seed know concerning us, how that we came out from Jerusalem," then "the gospel of Jesus Christ shall be declared among them," and only then the result, "their scales of darkness shall begin to fall from their eyes." The book is the first item in its own prophecy, and the effect described is a recovery of history before it is a conversion.

verses.label: v. 9–15
verses.title: Isaiah 11, printed twice in the same volume
verses.text: These seven verses reproduce Isaiah 11:4–9, which the volume has already given whole at 2 Nephi 21. Set the two side by side and four of them, verses 11, 13, 14 and 15 here, match 2 Ne. 21:5, 7, 8 and 9 word for word. Only two differ, and both changes are at the opening of the verse. Verse 9 supplies a subject where the earlier printing had a pronoun, "with righteousness shall the Lord God judge the poor" against "shall he judge the poor," and verse 12 replaces "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb" with "And then shall the wolf dwell with the lamb," which fixes the passage to a moment the surrounding chapter has just described.

verses.label: v. 10
verses.title: A division stated before the peace is described
verses.text: Between the judging in verse 9 and the wolf in verse 12 the record inserts a verse the Isaiah passage does not carry: "the time speedily cometh that the Lord God shall cause a great division among the people, and the wicked will he destroy; and he will spare his people." The animals lying down together arrive two verses after a separation and a destruction. A reader of Isaiah 11 alone meets the peaceable kingdom without that preface.

verses.label: v. 16–17
verses.title: Everything disclosed, stated three ways
verses.text: The record makes the claim once and then restates it twice in parallel negative constructions: "There is nothing which is secret save it shall be revealed; there is no work of darkness save it shall be made manifest in the light; and there is nothing which is sealed upon the earth save it shall be loosed." Secret, dark and sealed are three different kinds of hiddenness, and each gets its own verb. The same saying stands at Luke 12:2 and Matt. 10:26 in briefer form; here it is expanded to cover three cases.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: The last clause takes back part of what the verse gave
verses.text: The chapter ends on a limit: "Satan shall have power over the hearts of the children of men no more, for a long time." The first half is absolute and the qualifier at the end is not. Nothing in the chapter explains what a long time is or what follows it, and the sentence is the closing line of the book's prophetic section. The record states an end to the adversary's power and, in the same breath, declines to make it permanent.

chapter.title: The commentary ends where it began
chapter.text: Chapter 25 opened by explaining what the Isaiah block was for; chapter 30 closes by quoting from it and applying it to the restoration. The unit is bracketed by Isaiah, and Nephi's own contribution is the application in between.

chapter.title: Repentance replaces lineage as the criterion
chapter.text: Verse 2 is the most consequential sentence in the unit. Everything the book has said about seed, branches, remnants, and covenant people is subordinated to a condition any person can meet, and both named groups are subject to it identically.

chapter.title: Nephi warns his own people first
chapter.text: The chapter could have opened with the Gentiles, having just spent two chapters on them. Instead the first word is to his brethren, telling them not to suppose they are better. That order is the chapter's ethical center.

chapter.title: Restoration is described as removal
chapter.text: Four removals close the chapter and one addition. Verse 6: "their scales of darkness shall begin to fall from their eyes." Verse 17: "There is nothing which is secret save it shall be revealed... there is nothing which is sealed upon the earth save it shall be loosed." Verse 18: "Satan shall have power over the hearts of the children of men no more." The single positive statement, at verse 15, is quoted from Isaiah 11:9, "the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea." Even that arrives as filling, once the obstructions in verses 17 and 18 are gone.

chapter.title: The peace is dated and bounded
chapter.text: Many generations before the remnant becomes pure, a long time rather than forever for Satan's restraint. In a chapter that could easily have promised an unqualified end, Nephi keeps the qualifiers, which is consistent with the six-hundred-year specificity he insisted on in chapter 25.

chapter.title: Isaiah is used rather than expounded
chapter.text: Verses 9 and 11 through 15 are quotation without commentary. Having explained in chapter 25 that Isaiah is hard and that he would be plain, Nephi's final move is to set the prophet's own words down as the answer, which is its own kind of argument about what plainness was for.

applications.title: Check the comparison first
applications.text: Before reading any promise about your own group, ask whether you are holding it as evidence of being better than someone else. Nephi's first move in this chapter is to close that door on his own people.

applications.title: Apply the one criterion
applications.text: Take a person or group you assume is outside, and apply the chapter's actual test: are they repenting? The verse gives no other qualification, in either direction.

applications.title: Notice what is falling away
applications.text: The chapter's picture of new understanding is subtraction. Ask what has been removed from your seeing in the last year rather than what has been added to your knowing.

applications.title: Start with where you came from
applications.text: The remnant learns where they came from before they learn the gospel. Spend an evening on your own family's or congregation's history, on the chapter's logic that identity is the ground doctrine lands on.

applications.title: Say the hard verse with the soft one
applications.text: Hold the righteous judge and the great division in one sentence, as the chapter does. Practice describing God accurately when only half the description is comfortable.

applications.title: Let the qualifier stand
applications.text: When you make a promise or claim one, keep the limits in it. Nephi writes "for a long time" where he could have written forever, and the restraint is part of what makes the rest believable.

questions.text: Whose righteousness am I quietly measuring myself against?
If repentance is the only criterion, does my confidence rest on it or on something else?
What scale of darkness has begun to fall from my eyes, and what is still crusted over?
Which side of a great division would my current life put me on?
What am I keeping secret that this verse says will not stay that way?
Do I live as if Satan's power over my heart were already limited?
